entry.evidence: Elucidating such changes therefore requires a source-to-sink system more sensitive to climate than tectonics.

sequences.source_document: Publisher full text from XML (jats_text), with Figure 4 read from the PDF

steps.action: Frame the problem: if silicate weathering cannot explain erosion-climate feedback, a carbon sequestration mechanism independent of chemical weathering is needed.
steps.quote: Hence, erosional feedbacks on climate require carbon sequestration mechanisms independent of chemical weathering.

steps.action: Adopt from published work two candidate mechanisms: fluvial export and burial of organic carbon, and river nutrient supply boosting marine net export production.
steps.quote: [...] mechanism is the fluvial export of organic carbon from terrestrial landscapes to ocean sediment

steps.action: State the aim: use terrace and Bering Sea core records to link tectonically quiescent river incision, carbon export and CO2 drawdown at 2.6 and 1 Ma.
steps.quote: to elucidate links among tectonically quiescent river incision, carbon export, and atmospheric CO 2 drawdown across profound global climate changes at 2.6 and 1 Ma

steps.action: Recall the authors' earlier finding that Bering Sea sedimentation changes were synchronous with Fortymile River terrace incision pulses.
steps.quote: synchronous with pulses of continental river incision archived in two well-preserved strath terrace levels (T1 and T2)

steps.action: Select the Yukon River–Bering Sea system as a found natural setting where tectonic quiescence and crystalline bedrock make erosion sensitive to climate.
steps.quote: define a tectonically quiescent late Cenozoic erosional system more sensitive to climate than rock uplift or erodibility

steps.action: Map Charley River terraces T1, T2, the channel and a periglacial pediment in the field and on the 5 m IfSAR DEM, and measure gravel thickness and tread heights.
steps.quote: We mapped high and intermediate terrace levels (T1 and T2, respectively) and the Charley River channel

steps.action: Design isochron sampling, matched to the Fortymile chronology, of three T1 sites to test upstream age decrease and one T2 site to test a Middle Pleistocene transition age.
steps.quote: we sampled three sites on T1 (Figs. A1–A3) to test whether the terrace age decreases upstream

steps.action: Prepare 19 quartz samples and measure 26Al and 10Be by AMS at the Purdue laboratory, subtracting blanks and propagating blank uncertainty.
steps.quote: corrected each measurement for backgrounds by subtracting blank measurements

steps.action: Fit linearized burial isochrons (Zhao et al. 2016) to the 26Al and 10Be concentrations at each site to estimate burial ages.
steps.quote: We use the isochron approach of Zhao et al. (2016) that applies a linearization factor to correct post-burial production

steps.action: Check the common pre-burial history premise: all samples fall within 2σ of the regression lines, so no outliers are removed.
steps.quote: All 19 of the isotope concentration pairs plotted within 2 σ of the regression lines; hence none were omitted

steps.action: Build a revised U1341 age–depth model by fitting five OLS segments to published age–depth data, and derive linear sedimentation rates and constituent ages.
steps.quote: we visually identified linear segments ( n = 5 ) in the plotted age and depth data, and fit ordinary least squares regression models

steps.action: Compare the revised age–depth model with the published Horikawa et al. (2015) model and find a close match.
steps.quote: modestly revise an age–depth model that closely matches that of Horikawa et al. (2015)

steps.action: Estimate the organic matter source from C/N endmember mixing (marine 5.4, terrestrial 19), giving about 85 % marine-derived organic matter.
steps.quote: imply organic matter predominantly ( ∼ 85 %) derived from marine NEP

steps.action: Vary the terrestrial endmember to the measured Yukon suspended-sediment C/N of 11.3, which instead gives about 86 % terrigenous organic carbon.
steps.quote: and thus indicate a higher average proportion of terrigenous organic carbon ( ∼ 86 %)

steps.action: Compute TOC and Sixs mass accumulation rates from weight percent, a mean shipboard grain density and LSR, propagating uncertainties in quadrature.
steps.quote: We compute mass accumulation rates (MARs, g cm - 2 kyr - 1 ) for TOC and Si x s

steps.action: Compare the burial ages with the designed tests: T1 ages decrease upstream (2.2, 1.8, 1.6 Ma) and T2 dates to 1.1 Ma, within the Middle Pleistocene transition.
steps.quote: that decrease upstream on high terrace T1 from 2.2 ± 0.3 Ma near the Yukon–Charley River confluence

steps.action: Set the new Charley chronology against independently dated Fortymile, Klondike and Birch Creek terrace records and find close agreement.
steps.quote: Our Charley River incision chronology closely matches previously established Fortymile (Bender et al., 2020), Klondike River

steps.action: Derive incision propagation rates from terrace height–age data: about 160 mm/kyr on the Charley River and about 625 mm/kyr regionally.
steps.quote: Charley River incision propagated ∼ 140 km upstream at ∼ 160 mm kyr - 1 from 2.2 to 1.6 Ma

steps.action: Keep the regional claim of two climate-modulated incision pulses (2.6 and 1.1 Ma) that interrupt aggradation.
steps.quote: Taken together, these terrace chronologies demonstrate climate-modulated pulses of central Yukon River incision that disrupt regional aggradation.

steps.action: Compare the first incision pulse with U1341 records: provenance shifts to the Yukon, LSR triples, and Sixs and TOC MARs rise 2–4-fold at 2.6–2.1 Ma (Figure 4, p. 1047).
steps.quote: Synchronous with the initial incision pulse, from 2.6–2.1 Ma Bering Sea sediment

steps.action: Pose Yukon incision, linked through provenance indicators, as an alternative to the published North Pacific nutrient leakage explanation for increased productivity.
steps.quote: provides an alternative explanation to the prior interpretations of North Pacific nutrient leakage as a driver of increased Si x s MAR

steps.action: Compare the second incision pulse with doubled sedimentation, provenance shift and doubled MARs at 1.1–0.8 Ma (Figure 4, p. 1047).
steps.quote: the rate of Bering Sea sedimentation doubled between 1.1 and 0.8 Ma

steps.action: Keep the coupling claim on consistent timing: incision increased carbon sequestration both by terrestrial organic carbon burial and by boosting marine NEP.
steps.quote: Consistent timing among these records strongly suggests that Yukon River incision and sediment export increased Bering Sea carbon sequestration

steps.action: Check the mixed-source organic matter interpretation against the independent C/N record at shelf site U1343, which shows up to 40 % terrigenous matter.
steps.quote: consistent with our C / N ratio-based interpretation of mixed terrestrial and marine organic sediment sources since 4.3 Ma at U1341

steps.action: Compare the pulse timing with published boron-isotope and alkenone pCO2 reconstructions, which show a drop of more than 100 ppm near 2.4 Ma and a smaller, inconsistent drop near 1 Ma.
steps.quote: Some but not all p CO 2 records dip during the second pulse, with a decrease of 25–30 ppm

steps.action: Propose that fluvial-erosion-driven carbon burial and NEP, in systems like the Yukon worldwide, may have contributed to the pCO2 drawdown.
steps.quote: Decreased p CO 2 during these late Cenozoic climate changes may reflect enhanced terrestrial carbon burial and marine NEP

steps.action: Conclude that Yukon incision controlled organic carbon and nutrient export and sequestration in the Bering Sea; the global pCO2 link is left conditional.
steps.quote: This coupling strongly suggests that Yukon River incision controlled terrigenous organic carbon and nutrient export to the Bering Sea

steps.quote: Please state the objectives of the paper more clearly at the end of the Introduction.

steps.action: Rewrite the start of Methods 3.2 to explain the isochron burial principle and its sampling requirements.
steps.quote: How does 26Al/10Be isochron burial methods work (in a few words)?

steps.action: Soften the early statement of findings at the end of section 2.
steps.quote: I feel that the final findings of the paper are announced too early here

steps.action: Make explicit the C/N endmember mixing scheme (5.4 marine, 19 terrestrial) behind the 85 % marine estimate.
steps.quote: How did you quantify that 85 % of the organic matter is of marine origin? Was a mixing model used?

steps.action: Split and simplify the sampling-strategy sentence, recasting the T2 aim as determining whether the terrace dates to the mid-Pleistocene transition.
steps.quote: This sentence is hard to follow (e.g. “test whether” is used twice). Can you simplify?

steps.action: Decline a tense edit in Methods to keep the past tense consistent.
steps.quote: we prefer to not change “measured” to “measure” as suggested

steps.action: Referee 1 endorses the incision record and the conclusion and requests no revisions.
steps.quote: I do not have any comments for revision.

end.claim: Climate-forced Yukon River incision pulses at about 2.6 and 1.1 Ma controlled terrigenous organic carbon and nutrient export to the Bering Sea, and thus carbon sequestration by burial and marine NEP.

decisive_move.sentence: Setting the terrace incision chronologies against the re-modelled U1341 provenance and mass-accumulation records showed synchronous pulses, and the coupling claim rests on this timing match.

gates.evidence: Action: the Charley sampling was designed to test predictions from the Fortymile chronology (upstream age decrease, T2 at the Middle Pleistocene transition), but all Bering Sea data are published compilations not acquired under the hypothesis (§3.2 ¶2, §3.3 ¶1). Claim: the new ages could have failed to match the regional pulses (§4.1 ¶1, §4.2 ¶1); the carbon-coupling claim rests on timing coincidence, and no rival prediction (nutrient leakage) was tested (§4.3 ¶1). Registration: the test aims are stated as set at sampling design, but there is no preregistration record.

imports.item: Accelerator mass spectrometry of 26Al/27Al and 10Be/9Be at the Purdue rare isotope measurement laboratory
Laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry for quartz purity testing
Piecewise ordinary least squares regression with standard errors for the age–depth model
C/N endmember mixing ratios for organic matter source (Perdue and Koprivnjak 2007)

novelty_claims.quote: [...] the previously unknown Pleistocene incision history of the Charley River (Fig. 2).

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: the Charley River burial ages and incision rates are estimate_with_resolution (§4.1 ¶1, §4.2 ¶1); the regional two-pulse incision is best_explanation across found tributary records (§4.2 ¶2); the link to global pCO2 drawdown is an untested hypothesis (status none; §4.4 ¶1, §5 ¶1). The alternative Yukon C/N endmember gives about 86 % terrigenous organic carbon, yet the conclusion keeps 'TOC (∼ 85 % marine)'; the paper does not reconcile the two (§3.3 ¶1, §5 ¶1). Inference: this alternative endmember sentence appears in the published text but not in the author reply (AC2-S p.2), so it was probably added during revision with no recorded request. Bering Sea data are all re-used published data; the age–depth segments were picked visually; weight-percent uncertainty was assumed negligible. The nutrient-leakage rival is set aside by provenance argument, not by a discriminating test; no lead–lag analysis is reported. The first sentence of §4.4 ¶1 is garbled in the published text. No supplementary sensitivity tests (e.g., to the 26Al/10Be production ratio) are reported. Earlier internal feedback (Bacon, Craddock) is acknowledged but not documented.

disagreements.target: The long-debated view that enhanced silicate weathering drove late Cenozoic CO2 drawdown (as reviewed by Hilton and West, 2020)
disagreements.support: Cited work shows silicate weathering is limited at high erosion rates and sedimentary-rock denudation releases CO2, so a weathering-independent mechanism is argued for.
